claim: Huovilainen derives the ladder stage from the transistor differential-pair tanh law, solves the resulting differential equation with explicit (forward) Euler, and obtains a cascade of four first-order IIR sections with embedded tanh non-linearities; only five tanh evaluations per sample are needed (table or polynomial approximation allowed). Euler was chosen because higher-order solvers need between-sample evaluations that clash with the feedback.

claim: Self-oscillation frequency: Zavalishin says the loop phase is -180 degrees at the cutoff and the resonance frequency approaches the cutoff as k approaches 4 (Sec 5.2, pp. 135, 137). Solving (1+s)^4 + 4 = 0 gives poles at s = +j, -j, -2+j and -2-j, so only the pair s = +/- j lies on the imaginary axis, i.e. oscillation at exactly the nominal cutoff (derivation by the agent, consistent with D'Angelo's pole-circle result, Eq. 7-9). With zero-delay feedback and prewarped g the oscillation therefore lands on the prewarped cutoff (inferred, not stated verbatim). D'Angelo says resonance frequency 'does not vary dramatically with k' for N = 4 (Sec IV.B) and gives no formula.

Zavalishin's analogue SVF (Eq. 4.1, p. 95): highpass y_HP = x - 2R*y_BP - y_LP, dy_BP/dt = wc*y_HP, dy_LP/dt = wc*y_BP; H_BP = s/(s^2 + 2Rs + 1) (pp. 96-97), the outputs satisfy LP + 2R*BP + HP = 1 (Eq. 4.4, agent's reading of the extracted statement that the three sum to 1). claim: Zavalishin's TPT SVF (Sec 4.4, pp. 109-111): y_HP = (x - (2R+g)*s1 - s2)/(1 + 2Rg + g^2) (Eq. 4.14, p. 110) with prewarped g; the denominator is positive for g > 0 and R > -1 so there is no instantaneous instability; precompute d = 1/(1+2Rg+g^2) and g1 = 2R+g; a band-pass-only version needs 3 multiplications and 5 additions: BP = (g*(x - s2) + s1)*d, BP2 = 2*BP, s1 <- BP2 - s1, s2 <- s2 + g*BP2 (p. 111). The normalised band-pass H_BP1 = 2R*H_BP has unit gain at cutoff (Eq. 4.15, pp. 111-112).

Stability under modulation: Zavalishin shows by time-warping (Eq. 2.28, Sec 2.16 p. 42) that cutoff modulation cannot destroy the stability of a structure in which equal cutoff gains precede the integrators, and that for a one-pole filter the output stays bounded by the input when the cutoff is positive (p. 43); for other parameters in feedback loops there is no easy general criterion and destabilising modulation does occur (p. 43); discretisation needs its own stability proof (fn 29, p. 42). A direct-form-II one-pole is judged inferior to TPT under cutoff modulation (Fig. 3.34, pp. 80-81).

claim: Eichas et al. model the MXR Phase 90: an input follower lifting the signal to about 5 V, four first-order all-pass stages using JFETs as voltage-controlled resistors, a mixer with the dry signal; stage centre frequency f_c = 1/(2*pi*(R_fix || R_JFET)*C_fix) (Eq. 17, DAFX-4); the JFET characteristic was measured (V_DS in [-2, 2] V, V_GS in [-2.8, -1.5] V) and stored as look-up tables; feedback resistor R15 inside the chain is optional (absent in the 1974 version) and adds resonance and harmonic distortion; the LFO is replaced by a triangular voltage source; matched JFETs are needed; the paper states no sample rate or oversampling.

Feedback is drawn around the whole chain through a unit delay (Fig. 1); the model did not reproduce the measured feedback response and the authors suggest delay-free-loop techniques (Sec 5-6, DAFX-37/38).

claim: Ideal ring modulation is multiplication of carrier and modulator, both centred on 0 V, and the output then contains only the sum and difference frequencies (Parker Sec 1, DAFX-1). For sine carrier and a sine input of frequency f, the product is a half-amplitude pair at fc+f and |fc-f| with carrier and input suppressed (trigonometric identity, agent's derivation).

claim: Digital multiplication differs from the analogue diode ring: Parker's diode model uses the Shockley equation (Eq. 1, DAFX-2) and a three-segment piecewise approximation (Eq. 2, DAFX-3; vb, vL, h, example germanium 1N34 values in Table 1) and adds integer multiples of the modulator frequency around the carrier and odd harmonics; harmonics fall about 20 dB per octave, so oversampling is advised: about x32 for wide-band signals, x16 or x8 for a sinusoidal carrier with modulator energy below 4-5 kHz (Sec 3.2, DAFX-4), versus about x128 for earlier forward-Euler models (Sec 1).

claim: Aliasing of an ideal ring modulator: the sum frequency fc + f exceeds Nyquist when the carrier plus input bandwidth exceeds fs/2, so a sampled product aliases unless the input is band-limited or the product is formed at an oversampled rate (agent's inference; the sources read do not state this for ideal multiplication).

Valimaki, Pekonen and Nam: polyBLEP/integrated-polynomial-interpolation adds a polynomial residual (ideal band-limited step minus unit step) to samples around each discontinuity of the naive waveform; the fractional position is d = p(n)/(f0*T) with p(n) the modulo-counter value after the wrap (Eq. 12-13, p. 977); residuals are tabulated for Lagrange orders (Tables I-III, p. 978) and B-splines (Tables VI-VII, pp. 980-981); a second-order FIR equaliser b0 + b1 z^-1 + b0 z^-2 restores high harmonics within about 1 dB below 15 kHz (Eq. 16, Table IV, p. 979); even interpolation orders are recommended (pp. 979-980); no lookup table or oversampling is needed.
